text: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is the national space agency of India, headquartered in Bengaluru, Karnataka, and functions as the principal research and development arm of the Department of Space (DoS), which is overseen by the Prime Minister of India. The Chairman of ISRO also serves as the chief executive of the DoS. ISRO is primarily responsible for space-based operations, space exploration, international space cooperation, and the development of related technologies. It operates a constellation of imaging, communication, and remote sensing satellites and manages the GAGAN and IRNSS satellite navigation systems. The agency has conducted three lunar missions and one Mars mission. Formerly known as the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR), established in 1962 by then-Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru on the recommendation of scientist Vikram Sarabhai, it was renamed ISRO in 1969 and initially subsumed into the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE). In 1972, the Government of India established a space commission and the DoS, bringing ISRO under its purview, institutionalising space research in India. ISRO launched India's first satellite, Aryabhata, in 1975 via the Soviet Interkosmos launch vehicle. In 1980, it successfully launched the RS-1 satellite on board the indigenously built SLV-3 launch vehicle, making India the seventh country to achieve orbital launches. ISRO has since developed various small-lift and medium-lift launch vehicles, enabling it to launch satellites and conduct deep space missions. It is one of six global government space agencies with full launch capabilities, including the ability to deploy cryogenic engines, launch extraterrestrial missions, and deploy artificial satellites, and is the only one of four governmental agencies to have demonstrated unmanned soft landing capabilities. ISRO's programmes have significantly contributed to socio-economic development in civilian and military domains, including disaster management, telemedicine, navigation, and reconnaissance, and its spin-off technologies have advanced engineering and allied fields. ISRO adopted an official logo in 2002, featuring an orange arrow shooting upwards with two blue satellite panels and the name ISRO in orange Devanagari on the left and blue English in Prakrit typeface on the right. Modern Indian space research began in the 1920s with S. K. Mitra’s ionospheric experiments in Kolkata, followed by contributions from C. V. Raman and Meghnad Saha. After 1945, key developments were driven by Vikram Sarabhai and Homi Bhabha, who founded the Physical Research Laboratory and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, respectively. Early research included cosmic radiation, high-altitude testing, deep underground experiments at the Kolar mines, and upper atmosphere studies. In 1950, the DAE was established with Bhabha as secretary, providing funding for space research. The Aryabhatta Research Institute of Observational Sciences (ARIES) was founded in 1954, and the Rangpur Observatory was established in 1957. The launch of Sputnik 1 by the Soviet Union in 1957 opened opportunities for global space exploration. INCOSPAR operated initially within the DAE, with IOFS officers, including H. G. S. Murthy and Waman Dattatreya Patwardhan, playing key roles in developing sounding rockets and propellants. The Rohini series of sounding rockets began launches in 1967. Under Indira Gandhi’s government, INCOSPAR was replaced by ISRO, and in 1972, the DoS was established to specifically oversee space technology development. India joined the Soviet Interkosmos programme and launched its first satellite, Aryabhata, via a Soviet rocket. Efforts to develop an orbital launch vehicle began after mastering sounding rockets, with the goal of launching a 35 kg mass into low Earth orbit. After seven years, the SLV-3 successfully launched a 40 kg payload into a 400-kilometre orbit in 1980, making India the seventh country to reach orbit. The SLV-3 had two more launches before being discontinued in 1983. In 1985, ISRO established the Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) and began work on the Vikas engine based on the French Viking, with testing facilities established two years later. The Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle (ASLV), based on SLV-3, was developed to launch satellites into geostationary orbit but had limited success and was discontinued. Concurrently, the Indian National Satellite System (INSAT) and Indian Remote Sensing Programme (IRS) were developed, leading to a large constellation of multi-band communication, radar, optical, and meteorological satellites. The PSLV, introduced in the 1990s, had over 50 successful flights (except for its first flight in 1994 and two partial failures), enabling India to launch all its low Earth orbit satellites, small payloads to geostationary orbit, and hundreds of foreign satellites. Development of the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) began, but India was blocked by the US from obtaining cryogenic engines from Russia’s Glavkosmos, leading to the import of KVD-1 engines with limited success and the launch of an indigenous cryogenic technology project in 1994, which took two decades to complete. A new agreement with Russia provided seven KVD-1 cryogenic stages and a ground mock-up stage without technology transfer, used for initial GSLV Mk.1 flights. ISRO faced US sanctions from 6 May 1992 to 6 May 1994, and after the US refused to share GPS technology during the Kargil War, ISRO developed its own navigation system, IRNSS (now NaVIC). In 2003, Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee urged the development of lunar and crewed space missions. ISRO launched Chandrayaan-1 in 2008, the first probe to confirm water on the Moon. In 2013, the Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan), launched on PSLV, became the first Asian spacecraft to enter Martian orbit and the first country to succeed on its first attempt. The cryogenic upper stage for GSLV became operational, making India the sixth country with full launch capabilities. In 2014, the heavier-lift LVM3 rocket was introduced for heavier satellites and future human missions. In September 2019, Project NETRA was announced to address space debris and near-Earth objects. On 23 August 2023, ISRO achieved its first soft landing on an extraterrestrial body, becoming the first nation to land near the lunar south pole and the fourth to land on the Moon with Chandrayaan-3, the third lunar mission. The Vikram lander successfully touched down at 6.04 pm IST (12:34 pm GMT) near the southern lunar pole, a world-first. On 2 September 2023, ISRO launched its first solar probe, Aditya-L1, on PSLV. On 30 December 2024, ISRO launched the SpaDeX mission, pioneering spacecraft rendezvous, docking, and undocking using two small satellites. On 16 January 2025, the Mission Operations Complex verified a successful docking, making India the fourth country (after the US, Russia, and China) to achieve successful space docking. ISRO also successfully controlled two satellites as a single entity after docking. In May 2025, ISRO completed the final abort test for the Gaganyaan human spaceflight mission, scheduled for launch in early 2027. In August 2025, ISRO completed the first integrated air drop test for Gaganyaan, hailed by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh as a step toward self-reliance. On 2 November 2025, ISRO launched its heaviest communication satellite, CMS-03, aboard the LVM3-M5 rocket from Sriharikota, marking a milestone as all eight LVM3 missions achieved 100% success. On 24 December 2025, ISRO launched AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird Block-2 aboard the LVM3-M6 rocket, the heaviest foreign satellite ever launched from Indian soil, weighing 6,100 kg (13,400 lb). ISRO pursues space-based applications such as research, reconnaissance, and communications, designs and develops rockets and satellites, and conducts upper atmosphere and deep space exploration. It has also incubated technologies in India’s private space sector, boosting its growth. Vikram Sarabhai, as INCOSPAR chairman in 1969, stated that India’s purpose was not to compete with economically advanced nations in lunar or planetary exploration or manned spaceflight, but to apply advanced technologies to real societal problems. A. P. J. Abdul Kalam noted that critics questioned the relevance of space activities in a newly independent nation struggling with food security, but Nehru and Sarabhai had a clear vision: to apply advanced technologies to real-life problems to play a meaningful role in the global community. India’s economic progress has made its space programme more visible and active, aiming for greater self-reliance. In 2008, India launched 11 satellites, including nine from other countries, becoming the first nation to launch 10 satellites on a single rocket. ISRO operates two major satellite systems: INSAT for communication and IRS for natural resource management. The DoS, under the Space Commission, manages ISRO and other agencies and institutes. Antrix, set up as ISRO’s marketing arm, promotes its products, services, and technologies. A separate entity focuses on marketing spin-off technologies, technology transfer, and industry interface. ISRO has established Space Technology Incubation Centres (S-TIC) at the National Institute of Technology, Agartala (east), Jalandhar (north), and Tiruchirappalli (south) to incubate startups aligned with space missions, bringing together industry, academia, and ISRO for R&D. In 2021, ISRO and the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) established a joint framework where ISRO approves space research projects of mutual interest, and IIST’s Advanced Space Research Group (ASRG) gains full access to ISRO facilities, aiming to transform IIST into a leading space research and engineering institute. To reduce dependence on NORAD for space situational awareness, ISRO is setting up telescopes and radars in Leh, Mount Abu, Ponmudi, and a future site in Northeast India to cover all directions. The Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota already supports the Multi-Object Tracking Radar (MOTR). All telescopes and radars will fall under the Directorate of Space Situational Awareness and Management (DSSAM) in Bengaluru, which will collect data on inactive satellites and conduct research on active debris removal, space debris modelling, and mitigation. For early warning, ISRO launched a ₹400 crore (US$53 million) project called Network for Space Object Tracking and Analysis (NETRA), which will track atmospheric entry, intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), anti-satellite weapons, and other space-based threats. All radars and telescopes will be connected through NETRA, supporting remote and scheduled operations. NETRA will follow the Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee (IASDCC) and United Nations guidelines.

ISRO is establishing telescopes and radars in four locations—Leh, Mount Abu, and Ponmudi—to cover the North, West, and South directions of Indian territory, with a fourth location in Northeast India to cover the entire eastern region. The Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota already operates the Multi-Object Tracking Radar (MOTR). All telescopes and radars will be managed by the Directorate of Space Situational Awareness and Management (DSSAM) in Bengaluru, which will collect tracking data on inactive satellites and conduct research on active debris removal, space debris modelling, and mitigation. ISRO launched a ₹400 crore (4 billion; US$53 million) project called Network for Space Object Tracking and Analysis (NETRA) for early warning, enabling tracking of atmospheric entry, intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), anti-satellite weapons, and other space-based attacks. NETRA will connect all radars and telescopes, support remote and scheduled operations, and follow guidelines from the Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee (IASDCC) and the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOSA), aiming to track objects up to 36,000 kilometres (22,000 mi) in geostationary transfer orbit (GTO). India signed a memorandum of understanding on the Space Situational Awareness Data Sharing Pact with the US in April 2022, enabling collaboration between the Department of Space (DoS) and the Combined Space Operation Center (CSpOC) to protect space-based assets from natural and man-made threats. On 11 July 2022, the ISRO System for Safe and Sustainable Space Operations Management (IS4OM) was inaugurated at the Space Situational Awareness Control Centre in Peenya by Jitendra Singh; it provides information on on-orbit collision, fragmentation, atmospheric re-entry risk, space-based strategic information, hazardous asteroids, and space weather forecasts, safeguarding operational space assets and monitoring spacecraft with close approaches over the Indian subcontinent or those conducting suspicious manoeuvres or seeking re-entry in South Asia. On 7 March 2023, IS4OM successfully executed a controlled re-entry of the decommissioned Megha-Tropiques satellite by firing four on-board 11 Newton thrusters for 20 minutes each, involving 20 manoeuvres since August 2022 and consuming 120 kg of fuel, with final telemetry confirming disintegration over the Pacific Ocean, as part of compliance with international space debris mitigation guidelines. At the 42nd annual meeting of the IADC in Bengaluru, S. Somanath stated that the long-term goal is for all Indian space actors—governmental and non-governmental—to achieve debris-free space missions by 2030. Since the launch of Aryabhata in 1975, India has deployed numerous satellite series and constellations via Indian and foreign launchers; ISRO currently operates one of the largest constellations of active communication and earth imaging satellites for military and civilian use. The Indian Remote Sensing Programme (IRSP) comprises India’s largest collection of remote sensing satellites for civilian applications, placed in polar Sun-synchronous orbit (except GISATs), providing data in various spatial, spectral, and temporal resolutions for national development programs. Initial versions used the 1 (A, B, C, D) nomenclature, later divided into sub-classes such as Oceansat, Cartosat, HySIS, EMISAT, and ResourceSat, with all names unified under the "EOS" prefix in 2020. These satellites support optical, radar, and electronic reconnaissance, city planning, oceanography, and environmental studies. The Indian National Satellite System (INSAT) is India’s telecommunication system, consisting of multipurpose geostationary satellites developed and launched by ISRO to meet telecommunications, broadcasting, meteorology, and search-and-rescue needs. Since the first INSAT launch in 1983, it has become the largest domestic communication system in the Asia-Pacific region, jointly managed by DOS, the Department of Telecommunications, India Meteorological Department, All India Radio, and Doordarshan. The series was renamed from INSAT to GSAT, then to CMS from 2020 onwards. These satellites are also used by the Indian Armed Forces. GSAT-9, known as the SAARC Satellite, provides communication services to India’s smaller neighbors. The Ministry of Civil Aviation has implemented an indigenous Satellite-Based Regional GPS Augmentation System (SBAS), known as GAGAN—GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation—as part of a plan for civil aviation, with a Technology Demonstration System (TDS) completed in 2007 by installing eight Indian Reference Stations at airports linked to a Master Control Centre near Bengaluru. IRNSS, known operationally as NavIC, is India’s independent regional navigation satellite system designed to provide accurate positioning services within India and up to 1,500 km (930 mi) from its borders, with a position accuracy better than 20 m (66 ft) in the primary area, offering Standard Positioning Service (SPS) and Restricted Service (RS). Kalpana-1 (MetSat-1) was ISRO’s first dedicated meteorological satellite. The Indo-French SARAL satellite, launched on 25 February 2013, is a cooperative altimetry mission that monitors ocean surface and sea levels, with AltiKa measuring surface topography with 8 mm (0.31 in) accuracy and 2 km spatial resolution, surpassing the average 2.5 cm (0.98 in) of standard altimeters. During the 1960s and 1970s, India developed its own launch vehicles due to geopolitical and economic factors, creating a sounding rocket and by the 1980s achieving the Satellite Launch Vehicle-3 (SLV-3) and the Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle (ASLV), with supporting infrastructure. The SLV-3 was India’s first space rocket, with a failed launch in 1979 followed by a successful one in 1980, making India the sixth country with orbital launch capability. The ASLV, developed in the 1980s to enable geostationary orbit launches, faced repeated failures and was abandoned in favor of a new project due to insufficient funding. The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV), India’s first medium-lift launch vehicle, enabled the launch of all remote-sensing satellites into Sun-synchronous orbit; it failed in its first launch in 1993 and had two other partial failures, but has since become ISRO’s primary launch vehicle with over 50 successful launches placing hundreds of Indian and foreign satellites into orbit. The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV), conceived in the 1990s to transfer significant payloads to geostationary orbit, faced delays due to the development of the CE-7.5 engine, with the US blocking India from acquiring cryogenic technology from Russia, leading to India’s independent cryogenic engine development. The Launch Vehicle Mark-3 (LVM3), previously known as GSLV Mk III, is ISRO’s heaviest operational rocket, equipped with a more powerful cryogenic engine and boosters than the GSLV, offering higher payload capacity and enabling India to launch all its communication satellites. LVM3 is expected to carry India’s first crewed mission to space and will serve as a testbed for the SE-2000 engine for future heavy-lift rockets. The Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) is a small-lift launch vehicle developed by ISRO to deliver 500 kg (1,100 lb) to low Earth orbit (500 km) or 300 kg (660 lb) to Sun-synchronous orbit (500 km), supporting multiple orbital drop-offs for small satellites. Rohini is a series of sounding rockets developed by ISRO for meteorological and atmospheric studies, capable of carrying 2 to 200 kg (4.4 to 440.9 lb) between 100 and 500 km altitudes, with current models including RH-200, RH-300 Mk-II, RH-560 Mk-II, and RH-560 Mk-III, launched from Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station (TERLS) and SDSC Sriharikota. The Advanced Technology Vehicle (ATV) is a modified Rohini-560 sounding rocket developed to test a native dual-mode air-breathing scramjet engine; as of 2016, two test missions were flown. ISRO first proposed human spaceflight in 2006, leading to infrastructure and spacecraft development. A 600 kg (1,300 lb) Space Capsule Recovery Experiment (SRE) launched in 2007 using the PSLV safely returned to Earth after 12 days. In 2009, ISRO proposed a ₹124 billion (equivalent to ₹310 billion or US$3.7 billion in 2023) budget for its human spaceflight program, with an unmanned flight expected after seven years and a crewed mission after seven years of funding; however, crewed missions were not a priority for years. A 2014 space capsule recovery and a 2018 pad abort test preceded Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s 2018 Independence Day announcement that India would send astronauts into space by 2022 using the Gaganyaan spacecraft. ISRO has developed key technologies such as the crew module, crew escape system, space food, and life support systems. The Gaganyaan project, costing less than ₹100 billion (US$1.3 billion), aims to send two or three Indians to space at an altitude of 300–400 km (190–250 mi) for at least seven days using a GSLV Mk-III launch vehicle. The newly established Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC) will coordinate the Indian Human Spaceflight (IHSF) campaign, with an astronaut training center being set up in Bengaluru to train personnel in rescue and recovery, microgravity survival, and radiation environment studies. ISRO built centrifuges for launch acceleration preparation and will upgrade existing launch facilities at SDSC. HSFC and Glavkosmos signed an agreement on 1 July 2019 for astronaut selection, medical examination, and space training. An ISRO Technical Liaison Unit (ITLU) was to be established in Moscow to support key technologies and facilities for space life. Four Indian Air Force personnel completed training at Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center in March 2021. Axiom Mission 4 (Ax-4), launched in June 2025 by SpaceX from Launch Complex 39A at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center, included Shubhanshu Shukla as mission pilot, marking the first time an Indian astronaut traveled to the International Space Station (ISS). Shukla flew alongside Axiom commander Peggy Whitson and mission specialists Sławosz Uznański-Wiśniewski (European Space Agency) and Tibor Kapu (Hungary), with Prasanth Nair serving as backup and participating in training at NASA’s Johnson Space Center. Shukla spent approximately two weeks aboard the ISS conducting around 60 experiments, at least seven of which were developed by ISRO or Indian academic institutions, covering cognitive effects of screen exposure, microbial adaptation, muscle atrophy, and crop resilience in microgravity. According to ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan, Shukla’s activities will advance India’s Gaganyaan program. Media reports estimate the Government of India spent approximately ₹548 crore (US$65 million) on the mission seat, drawing scrutiny amid India’s efforts to develop indigenous human spaceflight capability; ISRO and Axiom Space defended the cost, citing value in astronaut training, operational readiness, and scientific return. ISRO is developing an orbital crewed spacecraft, Gaganyaan, for the Indian Human Spaceflight Programme (IHSP), designed to carry up to three people, with a planned upgraded version featuring rendezvous and docking. The first crewed mission will have a mass of approximately 3 tonnes (6,600 lb), placed in low Earth orbit at around 400 km (250 mi) altitude, supporting a crew of two for up to seven days. India plans to develop a modular space station, the Bharatiya Antariksh Station, with a mass of approximately 20 tonnes (44,000 lb), placed at 400 km (250 mi) altitude, initially supporting up to three astronauts for 15 to 20-day missions. The station is intended to be launched five to seven years after Gaganyaan’s completion and will be expanded in phases, serving as a platform for international collaboration in interplanetary exploration, microgravity science, space biology, and space medicine. ISRO and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research have operated a balloon launch base in Hyderabad since 1967, located near the geomagnetic equator where cosmic ray fluxes are low, making it ideal for studying diffuse cosmic X-ray background. ISRO contributed to the discovery of three bacterial species in the upper stratosphere (20–40 km), highly resistant to UV radiation and not found elsewhere on Earth, leading to speculation about extraterrestrial origin. These extremophiles are named Bacillus isronensis (in recognition of ISRO’s role), Bacillus aryabhata (after the ancient Indian astronomer Aryabhata), and Janibacter hoylei (after astrophysicist Fred Hoyle). Launched in 2015, Astrosat is a space observatory.

A platform for international collaboration in research related to interplanetary exploration, microgravity science, space biology, and space medicine exists. ISRO and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research have operated a balloon launch base in Hyderabad since 1967, benefiting from its proximity to the geo-magnetic equator, where primary and secondary cosmic ray fluxes are low, making it ideal for studying the diffuse cosmic X-ray background. ISRO contributed to the discovery of three bacterial species in the upper stratosphere between 20–40 km (12–25 mi), highly resistant to ultraviolet radiation and not found elsewhere on Earth, leading to speculation about extraterrestrial origins. These extremophiles are named Bacillus isronensis, Bacillus aryabhata, and Janibacter hoylei in recognition of ISRO’s role, India’s ancient astronomer Aryabhata, and astrophysicist Fred Hoyle. Launched in 2015, Astrosat is India’s first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory, observing active galactic nuclei, hot white dwarfs, pulsars, binary star systems, and supermassive black holes at galactic centers. The X-ray Polarimeter Satellite (XPoSat), launched on 1 January 2024 via a PSLV-DL rocket, carries the Polarimeter Instrument in X-rays (POLIX) to study the degree and angle of polarization of X-ray sources in the 5–30 keV range, with an expected operational lifespan of at least five years. Chandryaan missions are India’s lunar exploration series, with the first, Chandrayaan-1, launched on 22 October 2008 using a modified PSLV from Satish Dhawan Space Centre, entering lunar orbit on 8 November 2008 and operating for 312 days, carrying 11 instruments—five Indian and six from foreign agencies including NASA, ESA, the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, Brown University, and others—to map the Moon’s chemical composition and topography, especially its polar regions, and earning awards from the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, the International Lunar Exploration Working Group, and the National Space Society. Chandrayaan-2, launched on 22 July 2019 on a GSLV Mk III, included an orbiter, Vikram lander, and Pragyan rover, aiming to explore the lunar south pole; however, the Vikram lander crashed during descent on 7 September 2019 due to a software glitch after deviating from its trajectory at 2.1 km altitude, with telemetry lost seconds before touchdown; the orbiter successfully extended its service life to seven years. Chandrayaan-3, India’s second attempt to soft-land on the Moon, launched in 2023 and included only a lander-rover set, and on 23 August 2023, ISRO became the first space agency to successfully land near the lunar south pole, making it the fourth to land on the Moon; Prime Minister Narendra Modi declared August 23 National Space Day in India. The Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), informally Mangalyaan, was launched on 5 November 2013 and entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, becoming the first country to achieve Mars orbit on its first attempt at a record low cost of $74 million, with a launch mass of 1,337 kg and 15 kg of scientific instruments; the team received the 2015 Space Pioneer Award. Researchers from the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences and Indian Institute of Science identified Ladakh as the best site for India’s first Mars and Moon analogue research station to support mission planning and training, with studies led by Binita Phartiyal, Aloke Kumar, and astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla, focusing on geological and astrobiological research, human studies, crew training, technology readiness, and life support testing. A 21-day Mars and Moon analog mission led by Aaka Space Studio and ISRO will simulate extraterrestrial conditions, testing human health, biometrics, circadian lighting, and life support technologies, following prior simulations in the Rann of Kutch in 2023. On 2 September 2023, ISRO launched the 400 kg Aditya-L1 mission to study the solar corona, the first Indian solar coronagraph to observe in visible and near-infrared bands, with the primary goal of studying coronal mass ejections and their magnetic fields to understand space weather; it successfully entered its final orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point on 6 January 2024, approximately 1.5 million kilometers from Earth. Long-term plans include crewed landings on the Moon and other planets. Chandrayaan-4, a planned lunar sample return mission, is in its conceptual and design phases, expected to launch around 2028, returning up to 3 kg of regolith from near Shiv Shakti point, the landing site of Chandrayaan-3. The Lunar Polar Exploration mission (LUPEX), a joint ISRO-JAXA robotic mission, is planned for no earlier than 2028 to explore the lunar south pole, with JAXA providing the H3 launch vehicle and rover and ISRO responsible for the lander. ISRO aims to send an Indian astronaut to the lunar surface by 2040. The next Mars mission, Mangalyaan 2, is proposed for launch in 2030 and will include a rover, helicopter, sky crane, and supersonic parachute. ISRO is considering a Venus Orbiter Mission, approved by the Union Cabinet on 18 September 2024 under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s direction, with a budget of ₹1,236 crore (US$150 million), ₹824 crore (US$97 million) for the spacecraft, to study Venus’s atmosphere, surface, and subsurface processes, especially given its past habitability, and to understand planetary evolution; a payload called VIRAL, co-developed with LATMOS and Roscosmos, is planned. Conceptual studies are ongoing for missions to asteroids and Jupiter, with a launch window every 33 months and a Venus flyby required; development of RTEG power is being pursued to enable deeper space missions. AstroSat-2 is the successor to the AstroSat mission. Exoworlds, a joint proposal by ISRO, IIST, and the University of Cambridge, is a space telescope for exoplanet atmospheric studies planned for 2025, to be placed at the Earth-Sun L2 point, focusing on spectroscopy in the NUV-VISIBLE-IR ranges. The Indian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope (INSIST) will produce high-resolution deep UV-optical images and low to medium-resolution spectroscopy, recommended in March 2019 with seed funding and proposed collaboration with the Canadian Space Agency. DAKSHA is a proposed all-sky, high-energy transient mission to study gravitational waves and gamma-ray bursts from 1 keV to 1 MeV using twin LEO satellites with three identical instruments each, with seed funding issued and instrument development underway by teams from TIFR, IIT Bombay, Raman Research Institute, IUCAA, and PRL; ISRO has confirmed technical feasibility but has not approved funding. ISRO is studying a mission to the stable L5 Lagrange point, conceptually similar to ESA’s Vigil mission. A complement to Aditya-L1 is being proposed for a Low-Earth Orbit placement. A family of 50 artificial intelligence-based satellites will be launched between 2024 and 2028 to collect geospatial intelligence (GEOINT) using thermal, optical, and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) technologies, with AI-enabled satellites capable of communication and collaboration to monitor military movements and border areas for national security. ISRO is developing the Satellite-Protection Project to safeguard India’s space assets from threats, initiated after a near-collision in mid-2024. ISRO is developing more powerful and less polluting rocket engines, including the semi-cryogenic SE-2000 engine based on RD-120, which will be less polluting and more powerful than the Vikas engine, and when clustered with LVM3, will increase payload capacity; on 28 March 2025, ISRO announced progress in designing a semi-cryogenic engine with 2,000 kN thrust for the LVM3 booster stage. Reusable methane and LOX-based engines are under development, with methane being less polluting and requiring minimal refurbishment, with cold flow tests beginning in 2020. ISRO’s current launch vehicles lack the capacity to launch satellites beyond 4-ton class to geostationary orbit, a gap planned to be addressed by the Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV), a family of five modular medium to heavy-lift rockets, initially called Unified Modular Launch Vehicle, powered by LOX-methane engines, capable of lifting from 4.9 t to 16 t to geostationary transfer orbit—nearly four times the capacity of the existing LVM3. ISRO is studying heavy (HLV) and super heavy-lift launch vehicles (SHLV), with modular designs featuring interchangeable parts to reduce production time, and has mentioned an HLV with 10-tonne capacity and an SHLV capable of delivering 50–100 tonnes into orbit. A rocket family of five medium to heavy-lift class modular rockets, the NGLV, is being planned to replace existing PSLV and GSLV rockets. Two reusable launcher projects are ongoing: ADMIRE, a VTVL test vehicle, and RLV-TD, a program to develop an autonomous spacecraft launched vertically and landing like a plane. To realize a fully reusable two-stage-to-orbit (TSTO) launch vehicle, a series of technology demonstration missions are being conceived.

ISRO is developing a family of five medium to heavy-lift modular rockets, known as the Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV), initially referred to as the Unified Modular Launch Vehicle or Unified Launch Vehicle, which will share components and replace the existing PSLV and GSLV rockets entirely. These rockets will be powered by LOX-methane engines and have a payload capacity ranging from 4.9 tonnes (5.4 short tons; 4.8 long tons) to 16 tonnes (18 short tons; 16 long tons) to geostationary transfer orbit, nearly four times the capacity of the current LVM3. Two reusable launcher projects are underway: the ADMIRE test vehicle, a vertical takeoff and vertical landing (VTVL) system, and the RLV-TD programme, designed to develop an autonomous spacecraft that launches vertically and lands like an aircraft. To advance a fully reusable two-stage-to-orbit vehicle, a series of technology demonstration missions have been planned, with the RLV-TD serving as a flying testbed for technologies such as hypersonic flight, autonomous landing, powered cruise flight, and hypersonic flight using air-breathing propulsion. The first mission, the Hypersonic Flight Experiment (HEX), was completed five months after the RLV-TD's test flight in February 2016, which reached a height of 70 km and weighed around 1.5 tonnes (1.7 short tons; 1.5 long tons). HEX is intended to serve as a fly-back booster for the winged TSTO concept, followed by a landing experiment (LEX) and a return flight experiment (REX). India is transitioning from conventional chemical propulsion to Hall-effect and plasma thrusters to reduce spacecraft weight; GSAT-4 was the first Indian spacecraft to carry electric thrusters but failed to reach orbit, while GSAT-9, launched in 2017, used a xenon-based electric propulsion system for in-orbit functions, and GSAT-20 is expected to be India’s first fully electric satellite. On 28 March 2025, ISRO reported that its 300 mN xenon-based Stationary Plasma Thruster (SPT) successfully completed a 1,000-hour life test under 5.4 kW full power in a vacuum chamber. The electric propulsion system (EPS), incorporating SPT, is designed to replace chemical propulsion in future satellites for orbit raising and station-keeping, offering at least six times greater specific impulse, enabling satellite buses to carry more transponders, and will be validated in the next Technology Demonstration Satellite (TDS-01) mission. Radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs), also called alpha source thermoelectric technology by ISRO, use nuclear decay heat to power spacecraft; in January 2021, the U. R. Rao Satellite Centre issued an Expression of Interest (EoI) for a 100-watt RTG, which would extend spacecraft life and reduce mass compared to solar panels, enabling long-duration deep space missions to outer planets. Two radioisotope heater units developed by the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) were included in the propulsion module of Chandrayaan-3 and functioned flawlessly. ISRO plans to collaborate with the Department of Atomic Energy to use nuclear propulsion technology in future missions. On 27 January 2022, the Space Applications Center and Physical Research Laboratory jointly demonstrated quantum entanglement-based real-time quantum key distribution over a 300-meter atmospheric channel, including quantum-secure text and image transmission and quantum-assisted two-way video chatting. At the Indian Mobile Congress 2023, ISRO presented satellite-based quantum communication using quantum key distribution technology, aiming to counter quantum computers that could break current encryption. A significant milestone was achieved in September 2023 when ISRO demonstrated free-space quantum communication over 300 meters, including live video conferencing using quantum-key encrypted signals. The SSLV Launch Complex, under construction in Kulasekarapattinam, Tamil Nadu, will serve as ISRO’s second launch facility, primarily for launching the SSLV and private launch vehicles, with an estimated 20 to 25 launches annually, and is expected to be commissioned by December 2026. India’s satellite communication network, one of the largest globally, supports applications such as land and water resource management, disaster forecasting, weather forecasting, meteorological imaging, and computer communication, benefiting sectors like business, administrative services, and the National Informatics Centre (NIC). The Integrated Space Cell, under the Ministry of Defence’s Integrated Defence Staff, has been established to effectively utilize space-based assets for military purposes and assess threats to them, promoting cooperation among the three armed services and civilian agencies. India operates 14 satellites, including GSAT-7A for exclusive military use and the rest as dual-use satellites, placing it fourth in the number of active satellites in orbit, with GSAT-7A enhancing the Indian Air Force’s network-centric warfare capabilities by linking ground radar stations, airbases, and airborne early warning systems like the Beriev A-50 Phalcon and DRDO AEW&CS, and also supporting the Army’s Aviation Corps for helicopters and UAVs. GSAT-7, launched in 2013, was built for the Navy to monitor the Indian Ocean Region with a 2,000-nautical-mile footprint and real-time input to warships, submarines, and maritime aircraft, while GSAT-7A, launched in December 2018, supports the IAF’s network-centric operations. The RISAT series of radar-imaging satellites are used for military purposes, and EMISAT, launched on 1 April 2019, is a 436-kilogram electronic intelligence (ELINT) satellite that improves situational awareness by detecting hostile radars. India’s space programme has contributed to military spin-offs, such as the Agni missile, which was derived from the SLV-3 technology; A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, who led the SLV-3 project at ISRO, later headed the Agni missile programme, using the SLV-3’s solid fuel first stage and a liquid-fuel second stage derived from the Prithvi missile. The IRS and INSAT satellites were primarily for civilian-economic applications but provided military benefits; in 1996, the Ministry of Defence temporarily restricted IRS-1C use for border missile monitoring, and in 1997, the Air Force adopted space assets for surveillance and battle management. Institutions like the Indira Gandhi National Open University and Indian Institutes of Technology use satellites for education; between 1975 and 1976, India conducted the Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE), using NASA’s ATS-6 technology to broadcast educational content to 2,400 villages, significantly improving rural education. ISRO provides telemedicine services, connecting rural patients to urban doctors via satellite for real-time diagnosis, treatment advice, and follow-up at super-specialty hospitals, with mobile telemedicine vans deployed in remote areas. ISRO helped implement the Biodiversity Information System, completed in October 2002, which uses satellite remote sensing and geospatial modeling to create vegetation cover maps at a 1:250,000 scale, linking gene-level plant data with spatial information in a web-enabled BIOSPEC database for ecological hotspots such as northeastern India, Western Ghats, Western Himalayas, and Andaman and Nicobar Islands, through collaboration between the Department of Biotechnology and ISRO. The IRS-P5 (CARTOSAT-1) satellite was equipped with high-resolution panchromatic equipment for cartography, followed by IRS-P6 for agricultural applications, and the CARTOSAT-2 project, with a single panchromatic camera, succeeded CARTOSAT-1 by providing scene-specific on-spot images. ISRO has diversified its research into spin-offs, including bionic limbs, silica aerogel for cold-weather soldier protection, distress alert transmitters, Doppler weather radar, and sensors for engineering inspections. ISRO has signed formal cooperative agreements with countries including Afghanistan, Algeria, Argentina, Armenia, Australia, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Bolivia, Brazil, Brunei, Bulgaria, Canada, Chile, China, Denmark, Egypt, Finland, France, Germany, Hungary, Indonesia, Israel, Italy, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Maldives, Mauritius, Mexico, Mongolia, Morocco, Myanmar, the Netherlands, Nigeria, Norway, Oman, Peru, Portugal, Russia, São Tomé and Príncipe, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Spain, South Africa, South Korea, Sweden, Switzerland, Syria, Tajikistan, Thailand, Tunisia, Ukraine, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the United States, Uzbekistan, Venezuela, and Vietnam, and with international bodies such as the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), European Commission, EUMETSAT, European Space Agency (ESA), and SAARC. ISRO has two collaborative missions with France’s CNES: the retired Megha-Tropiques, which studied the tropical water cycle, and the active SARAL for altimetry, with a third mission, TRISHNA (a thermal infrared imaging satellite for high-resolution natural resource assessment), currently being planned. The Lunar Polar Exploration Mission (LUPEX) is a joint Indo-Japanese mission to study the Moon’s polar surface, with India responsible for providing soft landing technologies. NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) is a joint Indo-US radar satellite using dual frequencies (L and S bands), making it the world’s first radar imaging satellite to employ both frequencies. In India, the electromagnetic spectrum is auctioned to telecom companies; in 2010, 20 MHz of 3G spectrum was auctioned for ₹677 billion (US$8.0 billion). In January 2005, Antrix Corporation signed a deal with Devas Multimedia for 70 MHz of S-band transponder capacity on GSAT-6 and GSAT-6A for ₹14 billion (US$170 million) over 12 years, using spectrum allocated for satellite-based communication. If this spectrum were auctioned at the 2010 price, its value would have exceeded ₹2,000 billion (US$24 billion), a hypothetical scenario considered by the Comptroller and Auditor-General as a government loss. There were procedural lapses: the satellite capacity was allocated exclusively to Devas, violating rules requiring non-exclusivity; the Cabinet was misinformed about other service providers, and the Space Commission was not informed when approving the second satellite, whose cost was reduced to avoid Cabinet approval. ISRO committed ₹7.66 billion (US$91 million) to build, launch, and operate the two satellites. In late 2009, ISRO insiders exposed the deal, leading to investigations and its annulment; G. Madhavan Nair, then ISRO Chairperson, was barred from holding any post in the Department of Space, and several former scientists were found guilty of "acts of commission" or "acts of omission." Devas and Deutsche Telekom demanded US$2 billion and US$1 billion in damages, respectively. The Department of Revenue and Ministry of Corporate Affairs initiated an inquiry into Devas’ shareholding. In March 2015, the Central Bureau of Investigation registered a case against the then executive director of Antrix, two officials of a USA-based company, a Bengaluru-based private multimedia company, and other unknown officials under Section 120-B, Section 420 of IPC, and Section 13(2) read with 13(1)(d) of the PC Act, 1988. Devas initiated arbitration proceedings in June 2011, and in September 2015, the International Court of Arbitration of the International Chamber of Commerce ruled in favor of Devas, ordering Antrix to pay US$672 million (Rs 44.35 billion) in damages. Antrix opposed the tribunal award in the Delhi High Court.
